comparisons.intro: Each of these does some things well. This is where Unseenet chooses differently.

items.name: Discord
items.text: Discord is a company. It owns the servers and everything written on them, can read it, can close a server or ban you everywhere at once, and wants your email and often your phone number. It is built for chat, so longer discussions get lost in the scroll. On Unseenet nobody owns the network, you need no account, discussion groups keep their threads, and private conversations can only be read by the people in them.

items.name: Matrix
items.text: Matrix is decentralised and has good end-to-end encryption. But its servers stand at public addresses that can be found and taken down, your account belongs to one server, and that server sees who you talk to and where you connect from. On Unseenet everything goes over Tor, nodes cannot be located, and you are your key - not an account on someone's server.

items.name: Nostr
items.text: Nostr shares a good idea with Unseenet: posts signed with your own key, so no server decides who you are. But its relays run on the open internet and see your IP address unless you set up Tor yourself, and it is built mostly around public feeds. Unseenet always goes over Tor and is built around groups and threaded discussion.

items.name: Reddit and web forums
items.text: Reddit and forums still have real threaded discussion. But each one is a single website run by a company or a person, who holds your account, sees your IP address and can delete a community overnight. Chat and private messages, where there are any, are a side feature that the same owner can read. On Unseenet the groups are copied across many nodes, and chat, discussion and private posts are equals in one network - with the private ones encrypted end to end.

items.name: The old Usenet
items.text: Usenet is where the idea comes from. But anyone could forge who a post was from, nothing was encrypted, the servers stood at known addresses run by internet providers - most of whom have long since dropped it - and spam nearly drowned it. Unseenet keeps the groups, the threads and the quoting, and adds what has been learned since.

comparisons.title: How is it different?

paragraphs: Unseenet is a place for discussion groups and chats that nobody owns. You follow groups about the things you care about, read the threads, reply and quote - or just chat - much like on the old Usenet and the BBSes of the 1980s and 90s.

The groups live on nodes: small servers that anyone can run, on a Raspberry Pi or an old laptop. The nodes copy the groups to each other, so every group exists in many places at once. The name says it: Usenet, unseen.
sections.title: What is Unseenet?

paragraphs: Most places online now give you only one way to talk. Chat apps give you a stream of quick lines that scroll away. Forums and the old Usenet give you threads, but no chat. For anything private you need yet another app.

Unseenet has all three, in the same network and the same program. Chat groups for quick talk. Discussion groups where every post has its place in a thread, you can read one post at a time, and you reply by quoting what you answer - so a good discussion is still easy to follow a week later. And private chats and private posts for when it is just between you and someone else.
Each group's owner decides what the group is for, and your client always shows clearly whether you are writing a chat line or a post.
sections.title: Chat, discussion and private posts - in one place

paragraphs: Most conversations online now happen on platforms owned by a company. The company decides who may speak and what may be said, can read along, sells your attention, and can close it all down from one day to the next.

Unseenet is meant to be the opposite: a network that belongs to the people who use it and run it, where you can talk freely without handing over your phone number, your email or your name - and where nobody can see who you are unless you tell them.
sections.title: Why it exists

paragraphs: Everything Unseenet sends travels over Tor, an encrypted network run by thousands of volunteers. Your traffic is wrapped in layers of encryption and passed through three random computers around the world. Each one knows only the one before it and the one after it, so none of them knows both who you are and what you are doing.

The node you use does not learn where you are. Someone watching your connection - your internet provider, the café Wi-Fi, a government - sees only that you use Tor: not what you read, not what you write, and not to whom.
Nodes also wait a random while before they pass a post on, and they do not note which way it came. That makes it hard to trace a post back to where it was written.
sections.title: Nobody can see who talks to whom

paragraphs: Every node is a Tor onion service. It has an address - a long name ending in .onion - but no location. Nobody can look up where it stands, which country it is in or who runs it, and the node does not know where its visitors are either.

There is no central server and no company behind the network. If a node disappears, its groups live on at all the others, and anyone can start a new node in minutes. A country can forbid Unseenet, but there is nobody to order to turn it off and no single place to pull the plug.
sections.title: Servers nobody can find, a network nobody can switch off

paragraphs: No government, company or other powerful organisation can take control of Unseenet. There is no owner to pressure, no list of names, emails or phone numbers to hand over, and no record of who connected from where - because none of it exists.
Nor can they look up who wrote a post or where it was written from. The only one who can give away who you are is you: by your name, by what you write, or by who you tell.
sections.title: Out of reach of the powerful

paragraphs: This matters most to the people who need it most: whistleblowers who want to expose wrongdoing without losing their job or their freedom, journalists and their sources, people living where criticising those in power is punished, and anyone who has something to say that they cannot say under their own name.

Tools such as Tor Browser and SecureDrop already protect people like them every day. Unseenet wants to give them somewhere to talk together, not only a way to send a tip. But until Unseenet has been independently reviewed, they should rely on the tools that have been - see "Where it stands" below.
sections.title: A voice for those who must not be found

paragraphs: The first time you start Unseenet, your client makes a key for you. Think of it as a personal seal that only you hold, kept locked away in your vault.

Everything you write is stamped with that seal. Anyone can check the stamp, but nobody can make it without your key. So when a post says it is from you, it really is: nobody can write in your name, and nobody can change a single word of it on the way.

That was the weak spot of the old Usenet, where anyone could put any name on a post. On Unseenet your key is who you are. You need no account, no email and no phone number - and if you like, you can claim a name such as @yourname so people recognise you.
sections.title: A post from you is from you

paragraphs: Closed groups, private posts and private chats are locked on your own computer before they leave it (end-to-end encryption). The nodes carry them, but all they see is scrambled data. Only the people they are meant for can open them.
sections.title: Private means private

paragraphs: The client is one program with Tor built in. Put it on a USB stick and run it on Windows, macOS or Linux - or start the computer from the stick and run everything from memory.
Your keys, your groups and what you have read are kept in one encrypted vault. If you lose the stick, whoever finds it sees nothing without your passphrase.
sections.title: Your network in your pocket

paragraphs: Instead of accounts and a moderation company, every post costs your computer a few seconds of work. You hardly notice it; someone trying to send thousands of spam posts does.

Each group has an owner who writes its charter and can ban people from it, and hierarchies such as dk.* have maintainers who can stop illegal content such as threats. But nobody rules the whole network.
sections.title: No spam, no bosses

paragraphs: The protection that shields a whistleblower also shields people with bad intentions. Criminals and other shady people can use Unseenet too, and they are harder to find here than on a platform that knows everyone's phone number.

Unseenet cannot check anyone's age or identity - having no accounts is the whole point. So there is no age check, and in open groups you may meet things you did not ask for. It is not a place for children without an adult who knows what it is.

What there is: group owners can ban people from their groups, hierarchy maintainers can block illegal content such as threats across a whole hierarchy, and you decide which groups you follow. The law still applies to what people say and do; Unseenet only makes it harder to find out who did it.
We believe a free place to talk is worth that price, as Tor and encrypted messaging are. But you should know that there is a price.
sections.title: The other side of the coin

paragraphs: How Unseenet works is written down in open documents, the UN-RFCs, the way the internet's own standards are. Anyone can build a node or a client that works with everyone else's. The code is free software under the Apache License 2.0.
sections.title: Open, like in the old days

paragraphs: Unseenet is pre-alpha. The protocol may still change, and the code has not yet had an independent security review. Try it, pick it apart and tell us what you find - but do not rely on it yet to protect anyone whose safety depends on it.
And no network can protect you from yourself: what you write can still give you away, and Tor cannot hide you from someone able to watch the whole internet at once.
status.title: Where it stands - honestly

The official release notes: https://github.com/unseenet/unseenet-bootable/releases/tag/v0.5.0

Unseenet 0.5.0 now offers bootable images, making it easier to use the network on a USB drive. These images include the latest versions of the graphical and terminal clients, as well as Tor 0.4.9.14 from Alpine.

To use these images, simply download the appropriate version for your needs from the provided links. The graphical client is available in the `unseenet-gui-0.2.0-usb.zip` file, while the terminal client is in `unseenet-0.5.0-usb.zip`.

For more information and to download, visit [this link](https://github.com/unseenet/unseenet-bootable/releases/tag/v0.5.0).

message.body:
This is the demo of **Unseenet**: a discussion network in the spirit of Usenet and the old BBSes, carried over Tor. The people here are made up; the network is real.

Have a look around:

- **This feed** - what the people of the demo are up to. Comment on anything.
- **Their own feeds** - follow a person, and their posts come into your timeline.
- **The chat**, **the discussion group** and **the photos** next door.
- **The site** - pages that stay, with pictures and links.

Everything is reset every Monday, so try what you like.

GET /api/help/group-settings.intro: Every save is a new version of the group's manifest, signed with your key. What it says about posting applies to what is posted after it: what nodes already carry stays as it is. The type, the owner and the Group ID never change (UN-RFC 0004).

settings.affects: Readers: shown in group lists and searches.
settings.label: Title and description
settings.what: The name and the line shown under the group's ID.

settings.affects: Readers: clients only; nodes do not care. A reader may still switch.
settings.label: Shown as
settings.later: Change it any time; nothing posted changes.
settings.what: Threads (posts and replies) or chat (messages in order) - how clients show it by default (UN-RFC 0008).

settings.affects: Writers: nodes refuse other kinds in open, moderated and channel groups; in a closed group clients do.
settings.label: Takes
settings.later: Applies to what is posted after it; what is there stays.
settings.what: Posts with a subject, chat lines, or both (UN-RFC 0028).

settings.affects: Writers and nodes: nodes refuse files the group does not take, and each node decides whether it carries files at all.
settings.label: Files
settings.later: Applies to new posts; files already posted stay until they expire.
settings.what: Whether posts may carry pictures or files, which kinds and how big (UN-RFC 0027).

settings.affects: Readers and nodes: nodes refuse reactions the group does not take.
settings.label: Reactions
settings.later: Applies to reactions given after it; those given before stay.
settings.what: The view's default, none, any emoji, or your own set of up to 12 (UN-RFC 0048).

settings.affects: Readers who would comment; nodes enforce it.
settings.label: Comments
settings.later: Applies to comments after it; earlier comments stay.
settings.what: On a channel or feed: whether others may comment on what you publish, and for how many days after it (UN-RFC 0030, 0034).

settings.affects: Writers: higher postage takes longer to send. Nodes enforce it, and may ask for more than the group does.
settings.label: Postage
settings.later: Applies to what is posted after it.
settings.what: The proof-of-work every post here must carry, against spam (UN-RFC 0001).

settings.affects: Nodes: a suggestion; each node keeps what its operator decides.
settings.label: Kept for
settings.later: Change it any time; nodes follow it as they see fit.
settings.what: How long nodes are asked to keep posts (UN-RFC 0004, 0012).

settings.affects: Everyone here: quicker, but it tells more about when people write.
settings.label: Fast forwarding
settings.what: Nodes pass posts on without the random delay that hides when they were written (UN-RFC 0008).

settings.affects: Writers: shown, never enforced by machines - moderators act on it. Each reader's own rules decide what they see.
settings.label: Charter
settings.what: What the group is for and what it asks of those who write here, shown to people before they post (UN-RFC 0014).

settings.affects: Readers: each can turn them off; a hidden post always says who hid it.
settings.label: Spam reports here
settings.later: Change the list any time; readers' own choices stay theirs.
settings.what: Spam report issuers readers follow here by default, so spam is hidden from the start (UN-RFC 0045).

settings.affects: Writers: clients suggest them for new posts. Readers: found by language.
settings.label: Languages
settings.later: Change them any time; posts keep the language they were written in.
settings.what: The languages written here, the first the main one (UN-RFC 0052).

settings.affects: Readers: their clients and rules treat every post as having them, shown apart from the author's own.
settings.label: Tags
settings.later: Change them any time; they apply to every post, old ones too.
settings.what: Up to 8 tags every post here has - a topic, or a warning such as sexual (UN-RFC 0052).

settings.affects: Readers: each decides whether to use them.
settings.label: Labellers

GET /api/rules.help:
YOUR RULES - IN SHORT

One rule a line. Upper or lower case is the same.
# starts a comment, also after a rule.
Put # in front of a rule to take it out for a while.


WHERE A RULE APPLIES
A line in brackets; the rules under it apply there.

  [feed]       your feed (the timeline)
  [groups]     discussion groups shown as threads
  [dk.*]       groups whose name matches (* is anything)
  [all]        everywhere - also rules before any bracket


POINTS
Every post starts with score 0. A rule adds or takes points:

  +10 if author in following
  -30 if seen

per gives points for each of something, max sets a cap:

  +2 per time I reacted to author  max 20
  -1 per day old  max 30

What per can count:
  time I reacted to author   how often you liked this person
  contact who reacted        your contacts who reacted
  followed who reacted       people you follow who reacted
  reaction                   everyone who reacted
  reply                      replies to the post
  new reply since seen       replies you have not seen
  day old, hour old          the post's age


CONDITIONS
What comes after if. One of these:

  author in following        you follow the author
  author in contacts         the author is your contact
  author in ignored          you ignore the author
  author is "Sonia"          by name or key
  from a bot                 the author is a bot
  I posted in thread         you wrote in the thread
  I reacted                  you reacted to the post
  thread in watched          you watch the thread
  thread in ignored          you ignore the thread
  seen                       you have scrolled past it
  read                       you have opened it
  new replies since seen     it has replies you have not seen
  subject matches "text"     the subject contains text
  text matches "text"        the post contains text
  has pictures               it has a picture
  tagged linux politics      the author or the group tagged it
                             with any of them; tagged all ...
                             with every one
  labelled sexual nudity     a labeller you follow labelled it
                             so; labelled all ... for every one
  lang da en                 written in one of these languages
  group is dk.*              it is in a matching group
  older than 7 days          also minutes, hours, weeks
  newer than 2 hours
  score >= 10                the points so far
  reactions >= 3             also replies, new replies

Compare with  >=  <=  >  <  =  !=
Join conditions with and, or, not and ( ):
  +5 if author in contacts and not seen
matches finds the text anywhere, in any case.
It is not a pattern.


WHAT HAPPENS
Tested when all points are counted.

  show if score >= 0         show only these
  hide if author in ignored  hide these
  sort by score, then date   the order; also by reactions,
                             replies; add ascending to turn it

  blur if labelled spoiler    pictures and text behind
                             Show anyway (also in the feed)

In For you only, under [foryou] - nothing else acts there:
  quiet if for you is mention  listed, but not counted and no
                             notification; for you is reply too

In groups only - a reply never moves in its thread:
  fold if score < -20        closed, with its replies
  dim if score < 0           shown faded
  highlight if score >= 30   shown bold
  mark read if thread in ignored


A line that is not understood is skipped, and said.
The other lines still work.
Without rules the feed is newest first,
and threads are as they are.

# Your own rules - they run only here, and go with your identity.
# Lines starting with # are comments; a # in front of a rule takes it out.
# Without rules the feed is newest first and threads are as they are.

[feed]
+10 if author in following           # people I follow first
+2  per time I reacted to author  max 20
-30 if seen                          # what I have scrolled past, further down
+15 if new replies since seen
sort by score, then date

[groups]
+20 if I posted in thread
hide if thread in ignored
